name: Tomas Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work the hill country out of the Pinecrest depot. It's forest and steep valleys, so a lot of our lines run through trees, and half the job is keeping them clear and fixing what the trees break. A normal day, we're out at seven, chainsaws and climbing gear in the truck, and some days we walk a mile up a slope carrying a crossarm because no truck can get there. I like that it's real work, you're tired at the end and you know why. What wears me out is the winter storms, ice on the lines, and nights when you don't see your bed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to the work, and who's at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My father was a lineman out of the same depot for thirty-five years, and I started as his apprentice at nineteen. My wife Rosa works mornings at the bakery on Church Street, and we've got Daniel, who's fourteen, and Sofia, who's ten. Daniel's already saying he wants to be a lineman like me and his grandad. We've got a mortgage on a house my father helped me fix up, and about three months of money saved. I go to church most Sundays, I'm on the volunteer fire crew, and I don't touch any of that AI. I don't see the need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've always said, it's a lot of noise from people who've never held a chainsaw. Some city fellows got rich selling a dream, and that's that. I'd probably say it after church, not online, I'm not on any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means my life stays the same, and I'm grateful. The trees keep growing, the storms keep coming, and somebody has to go up that hill. That's me, and maybe Daniel after me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes. I'd keep working, keep putting a bit aside, keep fixing up the house on weekends. Maybe start teaching Daniel to climb properly, on the practice pole at the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a quiet Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Teaching Daniel to climb. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father did it with me when I was about fifteen, at the practice pole behind the depot, on a Saturday when nobody was around. I'd do the same. Daniel's strong and he's not scared of height, he'd do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about, even in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, maybe the women in the office if they bring in a computer for the bookings. But they'd find something. People round here help each other out.

S0.say: It's a lot of noise from people who've never held a chainsaw, and some city fellows got rich selling a dream. He'd say it after church, not online.
S0.think: His life stays the same and he's grateful: the trees keep growing, the storms keep coming and someone has to go up the hill. That's him, and maybe his son after him.
S0.do: Keeps working out of the Pinecrest depot, saving a little and fixing up the house on weekends. Starts teaching his son Daniel to climb on the depot practice pole.
S0.quote: Some city fellows got rich selling a dream, and that's that.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas's identity rests on family tradition: his father's trade and his son's plans to follow. He distrusts technology promoters and sees community as the safety net. He never uses AI and sees no need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should keep their heads down and keep working. Every generation has had something new. My grandad saw tractors come in, my father saw bucket trucks, and the world kept turning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit worried. If they start using drones to check the lines through the forest, that's some of our work gone. And they'd want us using tablets for everything, which I'm slow on. But you can't send a drone up a hill with a chainsaw to clear a fallen pine, not yet anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and see how it shakes out. If they made me use a tablet, I'd ask Daniel to show me, he's better with them. I wouldn't change much at home, maybe hold off on the new truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like seeing dark clouds over the next valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if jobs at the depot were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The managers in the city who've never been here, looking at a spreadsheet. And the big tech companies selling them on it. Not the government, I don't expect much from them either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change what you'd tell Daniel about becoming a lineman?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not yet. It's still a good trade, still needs a man or a woman who can climb and think. I'd tell him to learn the computer side too, because he can and I can't.

S1.say: People should keep their heads down and keep working, because every generation has had something new. His grandad saw tractors, his father bucket trucks, and the world kept turning.
S1.think: He'd be a bit worried that drones would take some line checking through the forest and tablets would be forced on him. But no drone can clear a fallen pine on a hill yet.
S1.do: Keeps working and waits to see how it shakes out, asking his son to show him any tablet he's made to use. Holds off on buying a new truck.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like dark clouds over the next valley.
S1.quote: My grandad saw tractors come in, my father saw bucket trucks, and the world kept turning.
S1.fieldNote: He places the change in a long family history, which steadies him. He blames distant managers and tech companies rather than government. He'd still encourage his son into the trade, with computer skills added.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disgrace, a handful of rich men in the city deciding everybody else is surplus. Nobody asked for it. I'd say families and churches would have to look after each other, because nobody else would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. I'm 43, I've got one trade, my father's trade, and if a robot can climb that hill and clear that pine, I'm finished. Three months of money and a mortgage. And Daniel's dream is gone before he's even started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut right back, no more takeaways, no trip to the lake this summer, Sofia's dance lessons on hold. Put every spare bit away. If I lost the job, I'd ask Rosa's brothers about work on their farm, and lean on church and family before I'd go to the government. I'd look for any outdoor work left, tree work, fencing, anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake listening to the rain and thinking about the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hardest part. I'd have to tell him the trade his grandad and I did might not be there for him. I don't know how I'd say it. I'd probably take him up to the practice pole anyway, just so he knows how it felt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go to church and family before government. Why that order?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they know you, and they don't make you fill in forms to prove you're struggling. And I'd rather owe my brother-in-law a favour than owe the state. That's how I was raised.

S2.say: It's a disgrace for a handful of rich men in the city to decide everyone else is surplus. Families and churches would have to look after each other, because nobody else would.
S2.think: He'd be scared: at 43 with one trade, three months of savings and a mortgage, a robot that can clear a fallen pine on a hill would finish him. His son's dream would be gone before it started.
S2.do: Cuts back hard, dropping takeaways, the summer lake trip and Sofia's dance lessons, and saves every spare bit. Would ask Rosa's brothers about farm work and lean on church and family before government, looking for any outdoor work.
S2.feel: Alarmed, lying awake listening to the rain and thinking about the mortgage.
S2.quote: I'd probably take him up to the practice pole anyway, just so he knows how it felt.
S2.fieldNote: His deepest pain is for his son and a family trade ending, more than for himself. He prefers community and family help over the state on principle. He blames wealthy tech figures for deciding people are surplus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for people to make their own plans, and they should. Work hard, save, look after your family. I wouldn't be waiting for some government scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is maybe worse in one way. Daniel would be nineteen, right when he'd start his apprenticeship, the age I started. He'd be training for a job that's about to disappear. I'd be 48 and in the same boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save harder, try to get to five or six months. Cut the extras now, not later. And I'd sit Daniel down and tell him to pick a different trade, or at least have a second one. That would break my heart, but I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. The extra time doesn't help much when it lands right on my son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What trade would you push Daniel toward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, that's the trouble. If robots do everything, what's left? Maybe something with people, like nursing, or the church. He'd hate that. He likes being outdoors like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the five years change anything for you, at 48?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit more money saved, a bit more mortgage paid. But I'm not going to start on computers at 48. I'd work until they told me to go, then find something outdoors. My father's generation didn't get handed a plan, and neither will I.

S3.say: Five years is enough for people to make their own plans, so work hard, save and look after your family. He wouldn't wait for some government scheme.
S3.think: Five years is worse in one way, because his son would be nineteen and starting an apprenticeship just as the job disappears. He'd be 48 and in the same boat.
S3.do: Saves harder toward five or six months and cuts extras now. Tells Daniel to pick a different trade or have a second one, despite how much it hurts.
S3.feel: Alarmed, because the extra time lands right on his son.
S3.quote: He'd be training for a job that's about to disappear.
S3.fieldNote: Unusually, five years felt as bad as two for him because of when it hits his son. He won't retrain himself and expects no plan from anyone. Steering Daniel away from the family trade is the hardest thing he can imagine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives everyone time to sort themselves out, so no excuses. People should learn a second trade, save, and keep their families close. That's what I'd say at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is the one I could live with. I'd be 53, with most of the mortgage paid, and I could probably work until near the end. Daniel would be twenty-four, old enough to have tried something and changed course if he had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, steady. I'd encourage Daniel to do the lineman apprenticeship if he wants it, but also something else alongside, maybe forestry or building. And Rosa and I would keep a bit more aside, so the kids have help if they need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but bearable. It's like knowing a hard winter's coming. You stack the wood and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why let Daniel do the apprenticeship in this picture, when you'd steer him away in the five-year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with ten years he'd get a good few years of real work, and the skills would help him in whatever comes next. Climbing, safety, working as a crew, you don't lose that. With five years, he'd barely finish before it's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change now, not later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably start keeping a closer eye on the money, writing it down like my father did. Not changing my job, just getting the house in order. Literally and otherwise.

S4.say: Ten years gives everyone time to sort themselves out, so there are no excuses: learn a second trade, save and keep families close. That's what he'd say at church.
S4.think: Ten years is the one he could live with: at 53 with most of the mortgage paid, he could likely work almost to the end. His son would be old enough to try something and change course.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving steadily, writing down the household money like his father did. Lets Daniel do the lineman apprenticeship with a second skill alongside and keeps more aside to help the kids.
S4.feel: Anxious but bearable, like stacking wood before a hard winter.
S4.quote: You stack the wood and get on with it.
S4.fieldNote: His feelings track his son's timeline as much as his own. With ten years, he sees the apprenticeship as giving lasting skills. He relies on self-reliance and family, not public schemes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The five-year one, if I'm honest, because of Daniel. The two-year one is worse for me, but the five-year one hits him at exactly the wrong age. What would help is keeping apprenticeships going for trades that still need people, and companies giving notice so families can plan. Not handouts, just a fair shot.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the storms. When the power's out in these hills and it's ten below, people need someone they know to show up. I don't think anyone up here would trust a robot to come in the night.

headlineQuote: I'd rather owe my brother-in-law a favour than owe the state.
portrait: Tomas Haddad is a 43-year-old lineworker in forested hill country, a lineman's son who started as his father's apprentice, with a wife who works at the bakery, two kids and about three months saved. He goes to church, serves on the volunteer fire crew and never uses AI, and he blames distant managers and wealthy tech figures rather than looking to government. He places mild change in a long family history, but fast AGI alarms him because his one trade and his son's dream would end together. Five years feels almost as bad as two because it hits his son at the start of an apprenticeship, while ten years lets him work nearly to the end and give Daniel lasting skills.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2031 worries him most, because it would hit his son Daniel at nineteen, just as he starts the apprenticeship, even though the two-year version is worse for Tomas himself.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping apprenticeships going for trades that still need people, and companies giving families notice to plan, rather than handouts.
